issues.legal_issue: Temporary residence at the place where a power of attorney is executed is sufficient to give the local registering officer authority to authenticate it, and residence does not depend on ownership of the place.
material_facts: The principal had been staying at the place where the power of attorney was executed for about a week and described himself as temporarily residing there.
He was there to complete loan negotiations, and other circumstances supported the finding that he was residing there.
The house belonged to a relative, not to the principal.
issues.conclusion: The principal was residing at the place when he executed the power of attorney, so the Registrar there had authority to authenticate it.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 33(1)(a) of the Indian Registration Act, 1908, “resides” includes temporary residence and does not require permanent residence or ownership of the premises. Residence connotes that a person eats, drinks and sleeps at the place, and whether a stay amounts to residence is a question of fact. The Court relied on Sharat Chandra Basu v. Bijay Chand Mahtab.

predicates.registration_validity_challenged: A party to a proceeding challenging the validity of a registered instrument disputed the authority of the officer who authenticated the agent’s power of attorney.
predicates.power_executed_in_officer_district: The principal executed the power of attorney in the district of the officer who authenticated it.
predicates.principal_resided_there_temporarily: The principal stayed, ate, drank and slept in that district for a period and in circumstances amounting to temporary residence.

issues.definition: When a registration-validity challenge concerns a power of attorney executed where the principal temporarily resided, the local officer had territorial authority to authenticate it.

issues.legal_issue: A power of attorney used to authorize an agent to present a document for registration need not itself be registered, and a mistaken or unauthorized earlier presentation of the power does not invalidate a subsequent, independent authentication by the Registrar.
material_facts: The agent presented the mortgage deed for registration under a power of attorney executed by the principal.
The Registrar examined the principal at his residence, satisfied himself that the power was voluntarily executed, authenticated it under section 33, and the principal signed before him.

An endorsement stated that the power had been presented for registration by another person, but the power was in fact authenticated rather than registered; the Court held that even an unauthorized earlier presentation would not invalidate the subsequent authentication.
issues.conclusion: The power of attorney was validly authenticated, and the endorsement mistakenly recording its presentation for registration did not invalidate the registration of the mortgage deed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 32(c) and 33 of the Indian Registration Act, 1908 require an agent presenting a document for registration to hold a power of attorney executed and authenticated in the prescribed manner; the power itself need not be registered. Section 32 applies when a document is presented for registration, not when a power of attorney is produced for authentication. A subsequent authentication under section 33 is an independent act and may remain valid despite an earlier unauthorized presentation. The Court relied on Bharat Indu v. Hamid Ali Khan and referred to the Bihar and Orissa Registration Manual rules distinguishing registration from authentication.

predicates.registration_validity_challenged: A party to a proceeding challenging the validity of a registered instrument disputed the agent’s authority on the basis of how the power of attorney had been handled.
predicates.power_used_to_authorize_agent: A power of attorney was used to authorize an agent to present an instrument for registration.
predicates.registrar_authenticated_power_independen: The Registrar separately examined or verified the principal and authenticated the power of attorney in accordance with the required procedure.
predicates.earlier_presentation_was_mistaken_or_una: The power of attorney had an earlier presentation that was either incorrectly recorded as a presentation for registration or was made by someone lacking authority.

issues.definition: When an agent’s authority is challenged because of an earlier mistaken or unauthorized presentation, an independent authentication by the Registrar leaves the power of attorney valid.

issues.legal_issue: An erroneous determination by the Registrar that a principal qualifies for authentication at a residence because of bodily infirmity is a procedural error that does not remove the Registrar’s authority or invalidate the authentication.
material_facts: The Registrar attended the principal at his residence and authenticated the power of attorney.
The principal acknowledged that an application for the Registrar’s private attendance may have been made but did not remember the reason stated.

The principal’s representatives argued that he was not suffering from bodily infirmity, but the application was not produced and the Court presumed that the Registrar had acted after satisfying himself that the required ground existed.
issues.conclusion: Whether the Registrar correctly found bodily infirmity was not open to challenge in court; even an erroneous finding would not affect his jurisdiction or invalidate the authentication.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 33(1), proviso (i), and sections 33(2)–(3) of the Indian Registration Act, 1908, a Registrar may authenticate a power of attorney without the principal’s attendance at the office in the specified circumstances. A mistake in deciding whether the procedural ground of bodily infirmity exists does not amount to lack of jurisdiction. The Court relied on Ma Pwa May v. Chettiar Firm and referred to Mujibunnissa v. Abdul Rahim for the distinction between procedural errors and jurisdictional defects.

predicates.registration_validity_challenged: A party to a proceeding challenging a registered instrument disputed the validity of the power of attorney used for registration.
predicates.registrar_authenticated_power_at_residen: The Registrar attended the principal at the principal’s residence and authenticated the power of attorney there.
predicates.registrar_determined_infirmity_requireme: The Registrar determined that the principal qualified for authentication without attending the office because of bodily infirmity.

issues.definition: When the Registrar authenticates a power of attorney at the principal’s residence after determining that the procedural condition is met, an error in that determination does not invalidate the authentication.
